title: Rotated vs Axis-Parallel: The Last Barrier
content: After BKU (2024) solved the axis-parallel case of Erdős #106, the remaining question is whether allowing rotation gives strictly better packings. This file formalizes the infrastructure to state and reason about this question.
mathContext: The axis-parallel problem: pack n unit squares in [0,1]² with sides parallel to the axes, maximize total side-length. BKU proved g(k²+1) = k. The rotated problem: same but squares may be rotated. f_rot(n) ≥ g(n) trivially; the question is whether strict inequality holds.

title: RotatedSquare: Parametrized by Center, Side, Angle
content: The RotatedSquare structure captures a square by its center, side length, and rotation angle. The interior is defined by rotating the test point back to the axis-parallel frame: p is inside iff rotating (p - center) by -θ lands in (-s/2, s/2)².
mathContext: RotatedSquare: center $(c_x, c_y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, side $s > 0$, angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$. Interior: $\{p \mid |r_x| < s/2 \wedge |r_y| < s/2\}$ where $(r_x, r_y) = R_{-\theta}(p - c)$ and $R_{-\theta}$ is rotation by $-\theta$.

title: Interior via Inverse Rotation: Coordinate Formula
content: The interior formula rotates the displacement vector (dx, dy) = p - center by angle -θ via the 2×2 matrix: rx = dx·cos θ + dy·sin θ, ry = -dx·sin θ + dy·cos θ. These are the standard rotation-matrix components for angle -θ, verifiable by noting cos(-θ) = cos θ and sin(-θ) = -sin θ.
mathContext: $r_x = \Delta x \cos\theta + \Delta y \sin\theta$, $r_y = -\Delta x \sin\theta + \Delta y \cos\theta$. This is rotation by $-\theta$: the point is in the interior iff $|r_x| < s/2$ and $|r_y| < s/2$, i.e., it lies in the $(-s/2, s/2)^2$ axis-aligned box.

title: GeneralPacking and g(n)/f_rot(n) as Suprema
content: GeneralPacking is a Fin n-indexed family with containment (closure ⊆ [0,1]²) and pairwise disjoint interiors. AxisParallelPacking extends it with angle=0. The objective functions f_rot and g_ap are defined as suprema of achievable sum-sets — this is the standard real-analysis approach when explicit maxima may not be attained.
mathContext: $f_{\text{rot}}(n) = \sup\{\sum_i s_i \mid (S_i) \text{ is a GeneralPacking}\}$, $g(n) = \sup$ over AxisParallelPacking. The supremum is used rather than maximum since it's unclear whether the sup is attained (compactness arguments would be needed).

title: Axis-Parallel ⊆ General: Trivial Direction via rfl
content: achievable_sums_subset proves that every axis-parallel packing is a general packing, so all achievable AP sums are also achievable as general sums. This immediately gives g(n) ≤ f_rot(n) via csSup monotonicity (proved in g_ap_le_f_rot at line 369). The proof is trivially one line: P.toGeneralPacking inherits from AxisParallelPacking extends GeneralPacking.
mathContext: $\{s \mid \exists P : \text{AP}(n), P.\text{sum} = s\} \subseteq \{s \mid \exists P : \text{Gen}(n), P.\text{sum} = s\}$. Combined with $\text{sSup}$ monotonicity, this gives $g(n) \leq f_{\text{rot}}(n)$. The actual inequality is in theorem g_ap_le_f_rot (line 369) using csSup_le_csSup.

title: The Three Area Axioms: Cauchy-Schwarz Upper Bound f_rot(n) ≤ √n
content: Three of the file's five axioms live here. rotated_square_area states that a rotated square of side s has measure s² (rotation is measure-preserving). f_rot_bounded asserts the Cauchy-Schwarz consequence f_rot(n) ≤ √n, and f_rot_mono asserts monotonicity. These encode the analytic upper bound rather than re-proving Lebesgue invariance under rotation and the full Cauchy-Schwarz/area argument from scratch. Together with bku_theorem_ap (line 513) and f_rot_2 (line 608), the file declares exactly 5 axioms — matching axiomCount in meta.json.
mathContext: Disjointness + containment give $\sum_i s_i^2 \le 1$ (areas fit in the unit square). Cauchy-Schwarz: $(\sum_i s_i)^2 \le n \sum_i s_i^2 \le n$, hence $f_{\text{rot}}(n) \le \sqrt{n}$. Rotation invariance of Lebesgue measure justifies $\mathrm{vol}(\text{interior}) = s^2$.

title: Edge-Midpoint Membership: Geometry Reduced to Coordinates
content: The AxiomElimination section eliminates what would otherwise be axioms by computing with the four edge midpoints explicitly. center_in_closure and the four midpoint_*_mem_closure lemmas show that the center and the points c ± (s/2)(cos θ, sin θ), c ± (s/2)(-sin θ, cos θ) all lie in the closure — verified by the Pythagorean identity collapsing the rotated coordinates to exactly ±s/2 or 0. side_mul_abs_cos_le_one and side_mul_abs_sin_le_one then deduce s|cos θ| ≤ 1 and s|sin θ| ≤ 1 from the fact that opposite midpoints, being in [0,1]², differ in a coordinate by exactly s cos θ (resp. s sin θ).
mathContext: For the +cos midpoint, $r_x = h\cos^2\theta + h\sin^2\theta = h = s/2$ and $r_y = 0$, so it lies on the boundary. Opposite midpoints have x-coordinates $c_1 \pm (s/2)\cos\theta$; both in $[0,1]$ forces $|s\cos\theta| = |(c_1 + \tfrac{s}{2}\cos\theta) - (c_1 - \tfrac{s}{2}\cos\theta)| \le 1$.

title: side ≤ √2: Key Geometric Bound via Edge Midpoints
content: side_le_sqrt_two proves that any square contained in [0,1]² has side ≤ √2 (regardless of rotation). Combining s|cos θ| ≤ 1 and s|sin θ| ≤ 1 from the midpoint lemmas, the Pythagorean identity gives s² = s²(cos²θ + sin²θ) ≤ (s cos θ)² + (s sin θ)² ≤ 2. This is the per-square bound that makes the achievable-sum set bounded above (next lemma).
mathContext: Opposite edge midpoints: $c \pm (s/2)(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. Both in $[0,1]^2$ forces $s|\cos\theta| \leq 1$ and $s|\sin\theta| \leq 1$. Then $s^2 = s^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) \leq (s\cos\theta)^2 + (s\sin\theta)^2 \leq 2$, so $s \le \sqrt 2$. The diagonal of a unit square is $\sqrt 2$, so this bound is sharp.

title: Achievable Sums Bounded by n√2
content: f_rot_set_bddAbove shows the set of achievable general-packing sums is bounded above by n·√2 — simply sum the per-square bound side ≤ √2 over the n squares. This crude bound (weaker than the axiom f_rot(n) ≤ √n) is exactly what is needed to invoke conditional-supremum lemmas like le_csSup and csSup_le_csSup: the supremum defining f_rot is over a bounded-above set, so it is well-behaved.
mathContext: $\sum_{i} s_i \le \sum_{i} \sqrt 2 = n\sqrt 2$. BddAbove of the achievable set is the technical hypothesis required for $\sup$ to satisfy $a \le \sup S$ (via le_csSup) and monotonicity (csSup_le_csSup). The tighter $\sqrt n$ bound remains an axiom; only boundedness is needed for the order-theory.

title: Explicit Constructions: Nonemptiness and g(n) ≤ f_rot(n)
content: g_ap_set_nonempty builds a concrete witness — n axis-parallel squares of side 1/(n+1) placed in a row along the bottom of [0,1]² — proving the achievable AP-sum set is nonempty (needed before taking its supremum). With boundedness (previous lemma) and nonemptiness in hand, g_ap_le_f_rot derives g(n) ≤ f_rot(n) from csSup_le_csSup applied to the subset relation, and g_ap_bounded chains this with the f_rot ≤ √n axiom to get g(n) ≤ √n with no extra assumptions.
mathContext: Witness: squares centered at $\left(\tfrac{2i+1}{2(n+1)}, \tfrac{1}{2(n+1)}\right)$ with side $\tfrac{1}{n+1}$, $\theta = 0$. Containment and disjointness are discharged by interval arithmetic on the x-ranges. Then $g(n) = \sup S_{\text{AP}} \le \sup S_{\text{Gen}} = f_{\text{rot}}(n) \le \sqrt n$.

title: Exact Values at Perfect Squares: g(k²) = f_rot(k²) = k
content: The heart of the proved content. g_ap_perfect_square constructs the k×k grid of side-1/k squares (indexed by i ↦ (i mod k, i div k)) and shows its side-sum is exactly k, matching the √(k²) = k upper bound — so g(k²) = k. The disjointness argument splits on whether two cells share a column (then rows differ, giving y-separation) or differ in column (x-separation). f_rot_perfect_square then squeezes f_rot(k²) between the √(k²) = k upper bound and the g(k²) = k lower bound, proving f_rot(k²) = k. This is why rotation provably cannot help at perfect squares.
mathContext: Grid: cell $i$ at center $\left(\tfrac{2(i\bmod k)+1}{2k}, \tfrac{2(i\div k)+1}{2k}\right)$, side $1/k$. Sum $= k^2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{k} = k$. Upper bound $g(k^2) \le \sqrt{k^2} = k$ gives $g(k^2) = k$ by antisymmetry. Squeeze: $k = g(k^2) \le f_{\text{rot}}(k^2) \le \sqrt{k^2} = k$.

title: BKU Axiom and Derived Bounds at k²+1
content: bku_theorem_ap encodes the Baek–Koizumi–Ueoro (2024) breakthrough as an axiom: for axis-parallel packings, g(k²+1) = k (one extra square cannot raise the optimal side-sum past k). The derived theorems package the f_rot consequences: f_rot(k²+1) ≥ k (at least as good as axis-parallel, via monotonicity from f_rot(k²) = k) and f_rot(k²+1) ≤ √(k²+1). These bracket f_rot at the first non-perfect-square value, where rotation could in principle help.
mathContext: BKU: $g(k^2+1) = k$. Derived: $f_{\text{rot}}(k^2+1) \ge f_{\text{rot}}(k^2) = k$ (monotone) and $f_{\text{rot}}(k^2+1) \le \sqrt{k^2+1}$. So $k \le f_{\text{rot}}(k^2+1) \le \sqrt{k^2+1}$, a gap of less than 1.

title: The Open Question: rotationHelps vs rotationNeverHelps
content: rotationHelps := ∃ n, f_rot n > g_ap n (rotation strictly improves). axisParallelSuboptimal restricts the witness to n ≥ 2. rotationNeverHelps := ∀ n, f_rot n = g_ap n (rotation never helps). Since g_ap ≤ f_rot is proved, rotationNeverHelps is precisely equality everywhere, and it is the logical complement of rotationHelps. The Erdős problem is to determine which holds — no example of rotationHelps is currently known.
mathContext: We have $g(n) \leq f_{\text{rot}}(n)$ always (proved). rotationNeverHelps would mean equality everywhere. Since $f_{\text{rot}}(k^2) = g(k^2) = k$ at perfect squares, any rotation advantage must occur at non-perfect-square n, with n=k²+1 being the most interesting case.

title: BKU Bridge: rotationNeverHelps + BKU → Full Erdős Conjecture
content: bku_and_no_rotation_implies_general (with helper rotation_never_helps_implies_conjecture) proves: if rotation never helps (f_rot = g globally), then the full Erdős conjecture erdos106GeneralConjecture, namely f_rot(k²+1) = k, follows from the BKU axis-parallel result g(k²+1) = k. The proof is one rewrite: rw [h] converts the f_rot question into a g question, then bku_theorem_ap closes it. This is the key decomposition separating a geometric question from a combinatorial one.
mathContext: Chain: rotationNeverHelps $\Rightarrow$ $f_{\text{rot}}(k^2+1) = g(k^2+1) = k$ (BKU). The general problem factors into a geometric part (does rotation help?) and a combinatorial part (axis-parallel packing). BKU resolved the combinatorial part; the geometric part remains open.

title: Agreement at Small n and All Perfect Squares
content: A cluster of agreement results pinning down where rotation provably cannot help: agree_at_1 (f_rot(1) = g(1) = 1), agree_at_perfect_squares (f_rot(k²) = g(k²) = k, restating the squeeze), and rotation_cant_help_at_perfect_square. The fifth axiom f_rot_2 encodes Erdős's original n = 2 argument (two disjoint squares in the unit square sum to ≤ 1), and no_rotation_help_at_2 derives f_rot(2) = g(2) = 1 by recognizing 2 = 1²+1 and applying BKU. So rotation is known to not help on {0, 1, 2} ∪ {k²}.
mathContext: $f_{\text{rot}}(1) = g(1) = 1$; $f_{\text{rot}}(k^2) = g(k^2) = k$; $f_{\text{rot}}(2) = 1 = g(2)$ via $2 = 1^2+1$ and BKU. These mark out the values at which the dichotomy is already resolved in favor of 'rotation does not help here'.

title: Boundary n = 0 and the Clean Dichotomy
content: The empty packing (Fin 0 → RotatedSquare) gives achievable-sum set {0}, so f_rot(0) = g(0) = 0 unconditionally (f_rot_zero, g_ap_zero, agree_at_0). rotation_helps_iff_not_never_helps establishes that rotationHelps and rotationNeverHelps are exact logical complements — the proof uses lt_of_le_of_ne with the proved g_ap ≤ f_rot to turn an inequality witness into a strict one. axisParallelSuboptimal_iff_rotationHelps then shows the 'witness ≥ 2' form is equivalent to the unrestricted form, using agree_at_0 and agree_at_1 to interval_cases away n ∈ {0, 1}.
mathContext: Empty packing: $\sum_{i \in \text{Fin } 0} s_i = 0$, so the achievable set is $\{0\}$ and $f_{\text{rot}}(0) = g(0) = 0$. Dichotomy: rotationHelps $\leftrightarrow \neg$rotationNeverHelps. Any witness $n$ with $f_{\text{rot}}(n) > g(n)$ must have $n \ge 2$ since equality is forced at $0$ and $1$.

title: Rotation Benefit Lives in [0, 1): A Sharp Quantitative Bound
content: The file's most distinctive proved result. sqrt_k2_plus_1_lt_k_succ shows √(k²+1) < k+1 (since (k+1)² = k²+2k+1 > k²+1), so f_rot_k2_plus1_lt_k_succ gives f_rot(k²+1) < k+1. Combined with f_rot(k²+1) ≥ k, this places f_rot(k²+1) in the half-open interval [k, k+1) (f_rot_k2_plus1_range). The benefit theorems conclude rotation_effect_unit_interval: the rotation advantage f_rot(k²+1) − g(k²+1) lies in [0, 1). So even if rotation helps, it can never gain a whole extra unit of side-length — it can at best shave into the gap below the next integer.
mathContext: $(k+1)^2 = k^2 + 2k + 1 > k^2 + 1$ for $k \ge 1$, so $\sqrt{k^2+1} < k+1$. Hence $k \le f_{\text{rot}}(k^2+1) < k+1$, i.e. $f_{\text{rot}}(k^2+1) \in [k, k+1)$. With $g(k^2+1) = k$ (BKU), the benefit $f_{\text{rot}}(k^2+1) - g(k^2+1) \in [0, 1)$.
